title: Identity & Access Management
description: Apply authentication, authorization, federation, least privilege, and account lifecycle controls to real cases.

questions.prompt: An accountant signs in to the company portal with the correct password and MFA, then receives HTTP 403 Forbidden when opening the payroll admin page. Which IAM process denied the request?

options.text: Authentication, because the MFA challenge was not satisfied for that page
Authorization, because her verified identity lacks permission for that resource
Accounting, because the audit log recorded the access attempt
Identification, because the portal could not determine which user she was

questions.explanation: She was already authenticated (identity proven); 403 means the server knows who she is but her permissions do not allow the resource. A failed or missing authentication would normally produce 401 or a login redirect, not 403.

questions.prompt: A company wants to require multi-factor authentication for VPN logins. Which combination actually provides two different authentication factors?

options.text: A password plus answers to two security questions
A fingerprint scan plus a face scan on the same laptop
A password plus a one-time code from an authenticator app on an enrolled phone
A password plus a second, different password stored in the user's vault

questions.explanation: MFA requires different factor types: something you know (password) plus something you have (the enrolled device generating codes). Security questions and a second password are both knowledge factors, and two biometrics are both inherence factors, so each of those is still single-factor.

questions.prompt: A help-desk analyst needs to reset MFA registrations for regular employees a few times a week. Currently the team plans to give her the Global Administrator role. Which option follows least privilege?

options.text: Assign a built-in or custom role limited to resetting authentication methods for non-admin users
Give her Global Administrator but require her to sign in with a hardware security key
Let her use her manager's admin account when a reset is needed, with the manager present
Give her Global Administrator during business hours only and remove it each evening

questions.explanation: Least privilege means granting only the permissions the task requires, so a role scoped to authentication-method resets for standard users is correct. Stronger sign-in or time windows still leave her with tenant-wide power she does not need, and sharing an account destroys individual accountability.

questions.prompt: True or false: NIST SP 800-63B recommends that organizations force users to change their passwords every 60 to 90 days.
questions.explanation: SP 800-63B (Rev. 3 and Rev. 4) says verifiers should not (Rev. 4: SHALL NOT) require periodic password changes; a change is forced only when there is evidence of compromise. Forced rotation pushes users toward predictable patterns such as Spring2026! to Summer2026!.

questions.prompt: Dana moved from Finance to Marketing six months ago. A quarterly access review shows she still has write access to the general ledger and the accounts-payable system. What lifecycle failure does this show, and what is the fix?

options.text: A joiner failure; re-run onboarding so her Marketing access is provisioned correctly
A leaver failure; disable her account and create a new one for her Marketing role
An authentication failure; require MFA on the finance systems she can still reach
A mover failure causing privilege creep; remove access not needed for her new role

questions.explanation: When someone changes roles, the mover process must revoke old entitlements as well as add new ones; otherwise access accumulates (privilege creep). She has not left the company, so leaver processing does not apply, and MFA does not fix excessive authorization.

questions.prompt: A hospital requires: clinicians may view a patient record only if the patient is admitted to the clinician's own department, and only while the clinician is on a scheduled shift. Which access control model fits this requirement most directly?

options.text: Discretionary access control, letting each record owner grant access to clinicians
Attribute-based access control evaluating user department, patient location, and current shift
Role-based access control with a single Clinician role assigned to all doctors and nurses
Mandatory access control with Confidential and Secret labels on patient records

questions.explanation: The decision depends on attributes of the subject (department, schedule), the resource (patient's current unit), and the environment (time), which is what ABAC policies evaluate (NIST SP 800-162). A single RBAC role would grant every clinician all records; pure RBAC would need a role explosion for every department-shift combination.

questions.prompt: Your service, https://api.reports.example.com, receives a request with the bearer access token below (decoded). The signature verifies against the issuer's published key, and the current time is 1790983800. What should the API do?

options.text: Accept it, because the signature is valid and the token has not expired
Accept it, but limit the caller to read-only operations because of the scope
Reject it, because the audience is a different API and the token was not issued for this service
Reject it, because RS256 tokens must be replaced with HS256 for API-to-API calls

questions.explanation: RFC 9068 and RFC 8725 require resource servers to check that aud identifies them; accepting tokens meant for another API lets any service that receives a token replay it elsewhere. A valid signature and unexpired exp are necessary but not sufficient, and RS256 is a sound choice, unlike a shared HS256 secret.

questions.prompt: A team is building a native iOS app that calls the company's APIs on behalf of signed-in users through an OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect provider. Which flow aligns with current guidance (RFC 8252 and the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP, RFC 9700)?

options.text: Authorization code flow with PKCE, launched in the system browser
Implicit flow, returning the access token in the redirect URI fragment
Resource owner password credentials, with the app collecting the user's password
Client credentials flow, with the client secret embedded in the app bundle

questions.explanation: Native apps are public clients, so they use the authorization code flow in an external user-agent with PKCE to bind the code to the app instance. The implicit and password grants are deprecated by the Security BCP, and a secret embedded in a distributed app is not secret; client credentials also authenticates the app, not the user.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of SP-initiated SAML 2.0 web browser SSO (HTTP-Redirect / HTTP-POST bindings) in order.

lines.text: User's browser requests a protected page at the service provider (SP)
SP redirects the browser to the identity provider (IdP) with a SAML AuthnRequest
IdP authenticates the user, or reuses an existing IdP session
IdP returns a signed SAML Response through the browser to the SP's Assertion Consumer Service URL
SP validates the signature, audience, and time conditions, then creates a local session

questions.explanation: In SP-initiated SSO the SP starts with an AuthnRequest, the IdP authenticates, and the assertion travels back through the browser via HTTP-POST to the ACS endpoint (SAML 2.0 Profiles). The SP must validate the assertion before establishing its own session.

questions.prompt: An auditor reviews accounts-payable entitlements against the company's segregation-of-duties rules. Which users hold a toxic combination of access? Select all that apply.

code.source:
User     Roles
jdoe     AP_Clerk (enter invoices)
asmith   AP_Approver (approve payments), GL_Reporter (read-only)
mlee     AP_Clerk (enter invoices), AP_Approver (approve payments)
pkim     Vendor_Master_Edit (create/edit vendors), AP_Approver (approve payments)
rkhan    Vendor_Master_Edit (create/edit vendors), GL_Reporter (read-only)

options.text: jdoe
asmith
mlee
pkim
rkhan

questions.explanation: mlee can both enter and approve invoices, and pkim can create a fictitious vendor and then approve payments to it; both let one person commit and conceal fraud. asmith only approves and reads reports, and rkhan's vendor maintenance combined with read-only reporting cannot move money.

questions.prompt: An audit finds 14 engineers hold permanent Global Administrator in the company's cloud tenant "in case they need it"; each uses it a few times a month. Which change addresses the finding while preserving their ability to do the work?

options.text: Keep the standing assignments but rotate the engineers' passwords every 30 days
Replace the 14 assignments with one shared admin account whose password is kept in a vault
Remove admin rights entirely and have the engineers ask the CISO to make each change
Make the role eligible-only, activated just in time for a limited period with MFA, justification, and logging

questions.explanation: Just-in-time privileged access removes standing privilege, so a compromised engineer account is not an admin account most of the time, while still letting engineers elevate when needed. A shared admin account removes individual accountability, and password rotation leaves the permanent privilege in place.

questions.prompt: Attackers are using an adversary-in-the-middle phishing kit that proxies the real login page, relays users' MFA responses, and steals session cookies. Users currently use push notifications. Which authenticator would defeat this technique?

options.text: Push notifications with number matching shown on the login page
SMS one-time codes sent to the user's registered phone number
FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys or security keys bound to the legitimate origin
TOTP codes with the validity window shortened from 30 to 15 seconds

questions.explanation: WebAuthn signs a challenge bound to the site's origin, so a credential for login.example.com will not produce a valid assertion for a lookalike proxy domain; NIST SP 800-63B Rev. 4 recognizes it as phishing-resistant and states OTP and out-of-band methods are not. Number matching stops push fatigue, but a user on the proxy page still sees and enters the number in real time.

questions.prompt: A contractor's account was disabled in the IdP at 09:00. Logs show his laptop kept calling the orders API successfully until 08:40 the next day. The API validates JWT access tokens locally (signature and exp only); tokens are issued with a 24-hour lifetime. What explains this, and what is the right fix?

options.text: IdP replication lag delayed the disable; schedule a forced directory sync at offboarding
Issued JWTs stay valid until exp; use short-lived access tokens and revoke refresh tokens at offboarding
The API skipped signature checks; enforce RS256 validation against the IdP's JWKS endpoint
The contractor's password was not reset; rotate passwords for all disabled accounts

questions.explanation: Self-contained tokens are validated without contacting the IdP, so disabling the account only stops new tokens from being issued; an existing token works until it expires. Short access-token lifetimes (minutes) plus refresh-token revocation, or introspection for sensitive APIs, bound that window; resetting a password does not invalidate tokens already issued.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS app supports "Sign in with" any customer's OpenID Connect tenant. After verifying the ID token's signature, issuer, and audience, it runs the code below. What is the security flaw?

code.source:
claims = verify_id_token(id_token, issuer=tenant_issuer, audience=CLIENT_ID)
user = users.find_one({"email": claims["email"]})
if user is None:
    user = users.insert_one({"email": claims["email"], "name": claims["name"]})
start_session(user)

options.text: Users are matched on the email claim, which a tenant admin can set to someone else's address; key accounts on iss plus sub
The ID token should be sent to the userinfo endpoint and its claims ignored, because ID tokens are unsigned
Users should be matched on the name claim instead, because it is set by HR and cannot be changed by tenants
The app should match on the access token's scope claim, since scopes are tied to a specific user

questions.explanation: OpenID Connect Core guarantees only that sub is unique and stable within an issuer, so the iss+sub pair is the correct account key; email can be mutable or unverified in another tenant, allowing account takeover (the 2023 "nOAuth" issue). Name and scope do not identify a user, and ID tokens are signed JWTs.

questions.prompt: A red team requested a Kerberos service ticket for the account below using an ordinary domain user, then cracked its password offline in three hours. Which remediation prevents this class of attack against this service?

code.source:
PS> Get-ADUser svc_sqlprod -Properties ServicePrincipalName, PasswordLastSet
DistinguishedName    : CN=svc_sqlprod,OU=Service Accounts,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com
Enabled              : True
ServicePrincipalName : {MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example.com:1433}
PasswordLastSet      : 3/14/2017 9:02:11 AM

options.text: Add svc_sqlprod to the Protected Users security group in AD
Require MFA for svc_sqlprod at every interactive logon
Mark svc_sqlprod as sensitive and not allowed for delegation
Migrate the service to a group Managed Service Account (gMSA)

questions.explanation: Kerberoasting works because any authenticated user can request a ticket encrypted with the service account's password-derived key and crack it offline; a gMSA's 240-byte random password, rotated automatically, makes that infeasible. MFA does not apply to service-ticket issuance, Protected Users is not intended for service accounts, and the delegation flag addresses a different attack.
